transcript:
Header:
Date: 2026-03-28
Start: 15:00 PT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Sofia Martinez (Redwood AE), Jordan Lee (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (Redwood ML), Liam Chen (Aurora CTO), Maya Patel (Aurora Lead ML Eng), Ethan Park (Aurora Infra)

Summary: Technical deep dive focused on quantization tradeoffs (INT8/FP8/GPTQ/AWQ), observed accuracy regressions, runtime impacts on latency/throughput, KV cache interaction, batching strategies, and VPC/on-prem deployment considerations. Agreed to run benchmarks and schedule pilot on dedicated capacity.

Topics: quantization accuracy, GPTQ vs AWQ, int8 inference speedups, fp8 considerations, KV cache effects, batching and latency SLOs, VPC/private deployment checklist, security docs.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sofia Martinez: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. We're here to walk through quantization options and how they map to your latency and accuracy goals.
[00:18] Liam Chen: Yep thanks. High level we care about 90th p99 latency under 350ms for our chat endpoint and want to reduce inference cost. We're running 13B models today.
[00:32] Jordan Lee: Great, that's helpful. Quick intro — I'm Jordan on the SE side, I'll share some perf numbers from Redwood's runtime. Also Priya is on for model-level questions.
[00:45] Maya Patel: Quick note — our main concern is regressions on our NER and extraction tasks, even small token-level deltas matter.
[00:58] Priya Kapoor: yeah, and we have a fairly long-tail of sequence lengths, so KV cache behavior is important.
[01:10] Jordan Lee: Understood. So we typically consider three quant paths: INT8 (per-channel or per-tensor), GPTQ-style post-training quantization, and AWQ-style advanced quant heuristics. FP8 is emergent but hardware support is still limited depending on the GPU.
[01:32] Ethan Park: When you say FP8 limited, do you mean on our cloud instances or on prem? We plan to test on both.
[01:40] Jordan Lee: Both — FP8 needs kernel support. On A100/A10X it's more mature; on older cards you might not get the acceleration benefits. Also on some private on-prem stacks the compiler/driver matters.
[01:52] Maya Patel: What's the expected accuracy hit for int8 vs GPTQ for a 13B?
[02:00] Jordan Lee: Good question. Roughly, naive int8 (symmetric per-tensor) can cause visible degrads on generation tasks — like 1.5-4% ROUGE or token-level accuracy drops depending on distribution. GPTQ tends to preserve accuracy better because it's per-channel and uses row-wise scaling with retraining-ish corrections. AWQ can sometimes match GPTQ accuracy while being faster to decode.
[02:24] Liam Chen: And runtime? How much faster is int8 vs fp16?
[02:28] Jordan Lee: On our runtime, INT8 optimized kernels give ~1.6-2.2x throughput vs fp16 for decode-heavy workloads. GPTQ/AWQ quantized weights with optimized kernels are in the 1.4-1.9x band — depends on KV cache reuse and batch sizes.
[02:45] Sofia Martinez: reminder — our serving runtime also does continuous batching and prefix cache. So your workload characteristics will affect realized speedups.
[02:56] Maya Patel: Can we talk about KV cache interaction? We saw some weird latency spikes when cache miss rates went up.
[03:04] Jordan Lee: Yeah — KV cache is a big factor. If your use case has long multi-turn conversations and high cache hit rates, token decode latency is dominated by attention compute on the last tokens and benefits a lot from quantized weights. But if your workload has many short requests (low reuse), batching efficiency and the initial key/value load cost dominates. Some quant formats store KV in a different layout which affects memory bandwidth and copy times.
[03:31] Ethan Park: That explains the spikes. We often have short synchronous requests under 10 tokens.
[03:36] Priya Kapoor: So for short requests, would int8 still help?
[03:40] Jordan Lee: It can help but less so. For <=16 tokens, the overhead of packing/unpacking and memory operations erode the compute advantages; end-to-end latency improvements may be modest — maybe 5-15% for int8. For long sessions with KV reuse, you see the larger 60-100% decode throughput gains.
[03:58] [00:04:00] Maya Patel: Are there known accuracy regressions with AWQ on extraction tasks? We've read some community notes.
[04:07] Priya Kapoor: AWQ tends to work very well on many tasks but there are corner cases. We ran internal evals where AWQ introduced subtle tokenization alignment issues for strictly token-level evaluation — often fixable with small calibration or using a higher-precision embedding layer.
[04:26] Jordan Lee: Yep — we recommend running your representative prompt set across the quant variants. For NER/extraction, token-level F1 is the metric we watch; sometimes GPTQ preserves that best. AWQ can be tuned (per-layer bit allocation) to match.
[04:40] Liam Chen: What about FP8 — is it promising?
[04:44] Jordan Lee: FP8 (e.g., E4M3 / E5M2 flavors) can give a nice sweet spot: near-fp16 accuracy with lower memory and some speedups, but it requires hardware/kernel support. And tooling for stable conversion is less mature; drivers can be shaky. Our recommendation is to prioritize INT8/GPTQ/AWQ now and keep FP8 on the roadmap if your infra supports it.
[05:06] Maya Patel: For GPTQ, do you provide artifacts or do we need to run offline quantization?
[05:11] Sofia Martinez: We can provide pre-quantized artifacts for common open models or assist you in running GPTQ. For Private/on-prem pilots you can run the process locally; we also have scripts that produce the quantized weights.
[05:24] Ethan Park: On-prem we have HIP/NVIDIA nodes, curious about kernel compilation.
[05:28] Jordan Lee: We'll share kernel build notes. For on-prem you may need to build a runtime variant if the OS / CUDA version mismatches. We have a compatibility matrix we'll send.
[05:39] [00:06:00] Maya Patel: Anything about batch sizes? We saw QoS drops with high batching.
[05:45] Jordan Lee: Yes. There's a latency vs throughput curve. Larger batches increase throughput but add queueing latency. Our runtime exponential backoff batching tries to prioritize SLOs: you can set max_batch and max_wait_ms. For your 350ms P99 target, we often keep max_wait_ms low (e.g., 8-12ms) and use smaller max_batch sizes for short requests.
[06:05] Priya Kapoor: Do quantized models increase memory pressure on GPU?
[06:09] Jordan Lee: They reduce memory for model weights, but some quant formats need extra bookkeeping tables or per-channel scales, so the net reduction varies. Also, certain kernels require temporary FP32 buffers during compute which can increase peak memory temporarily.
[06:23] Liam Chen: There was mention of calibration datasets causing drift — what's the proper calibration strategy?
[06:28] Jordan Lee: Use a representative calibration set that matches your prompt distribution. For GPTQ you often need a few hundred to a few thousand samples, depending on model size. AWQ may need layer-specific calibration. Avoid generic web text if your prompts are domain-specific.
[06:45] Maya Patel: Any advice on fallback strategies if quantized model shows regression in pilot?
[06:49] Jordan Lee: We recommend canarying: run quantized variant in parallel to fp16 on a subset of traffic, monitor your metrics; if regression exceeds threshold, automatic fallback policy can route to fp16 until issues resolved. Redwood's rollouts support percentage traffic split and auto-fallback.
[07:05] [00:08:00] Ethan Park: About VPC/private deployment — what does the network topology look like for dedicated? Can we keep key material in our KMS?
[07:13] Sofia Martinez: Yes, for Private deployments you control KMS and HSM. Dedicated can be deployed in your VPC with private subnets; our control plane can be segregated. We'll share the VPC diagram and the service account requirements.
[07:26] Liam Chen: Does quantization affect encryption-in-flight or at-rest processes?
[07:29] Jordan Lee: Not directly. Quantized weights are just different weight files; storage encryption (S3 or on-prem) and transit TLS still apply. If you use KMS for keys, the key handling is unchanged.
[07:41] Priya Kapoor: On evaluation, should we use log-prob deltas or downstream task metrics?
[07:45] Jordan Lee: Downstream task metrics — token-level F1, extraction accuracy, and human evaluation are the final authority. Log-prob deltas are useful for quick checks but don't always correlate with downstream behavior.
[07:58] Maya Patel: Could you walk through a concrete example of regression we might see after GPTQ?
[08:04] Jordan Lee: Sure. We had a customer where GPTQ introduced off-by-one token insertion in date parsing tasks — it was due to subtle rounding in softmax inputs for a particular layer; recovery required re-running with a different quant granularity on that layer.
[08:22] Sophia? (note: minor mislabel) Speaker 1: uh-huh
[08:26] Jordan Lee: Sorry, that was me — shows how auto-transcribe sometimes messes with names.
[08:30] [00:09:00] Maya Patel: How long does quantization artifact generation take for a 13B?
[08:36] Jordan Lee: On a beefy machine with 8 A100s you can do GPTQ pass in a few hours; single GPU might take 6-12 hours depending on tooling. AWQ can be faster if you use heuristics; INT8 straightforward conversion is fastest.
[08:52] Liam Chen: For pilot scope, we want to test 2 models across 50k requests of our trace. Reasonable?
[08:58] Jordan Lee: That's perfect — it will give you statistical significance for token-level metrics and latency percentiles.
[09:04] Priya Kapoor: On observability, can we get token-level latency and per-model per-route breakdown?
[09:09] Sofia Martinez: Yes — Redwood Console provides token-level cost and latency breakdowns, per-route traces, and you can export raw traces. We'll ensure trace retention for the pilot.
[09:18] Ethan Park: Any gotchas with batch packing and KV cache warmup during tests?
[09:23] Jordan Lee: Ensure you run traces with representative user behavior; cold-starts and cache warmup can skew p99. We recommend a warmup phase before measuring. Also measure both cold and steady-state metrics.
[09:36] [00:10:00] Maya Patel: For our NER tasks, what metrics threshold would you suggest for acceptable regression?
[09:42] Jordan Lee: Typical threshold is <1% absolute F1 drop for initial pilot; if it's more sensitive, we can set stricter thresholds. We can instrument alerts in the pilot if thresholds are exceeded.
[09:53] Liam Chen: Are there any licensing issues with distributing quantized weights from open models?
[09:58] Priya Kapoor: Generally follow the model license; some models disallow redistribution of weights. We can help you run the quantization in your environment to avoid redistribution issues.
[10:09] Maya Patel: Could you summarize operational steps for pilot?
[10:12] Jordan Lee: Sure: 1) provide trace and prompt set; 2) SE runs quantization experiments (INT8/GPTQ/AWQ) and uploads artifacts; 3) Redwood deploys quantized variants to Dedicated pilot environment in your VPC or our dedicated pool; 4) run 50k request benchmark with warmup; 5) evaluate metrics and decide rollout.
[10:33] [00:11:00] Sofia Martinez: We'll include rollback plans and pricing for dedicated capacity in the follow up.
[10:38] Liam Chen: For pricing, is quantized inference cheaper under the same pricing table?
[10:42] Sofia Martinez: We'll structure pilot pricing to reflect estimated token-level savings; typically unit compute cost goes down as throughput improves. We'll send a model of expected savings based on your trace.
[10:52] Maya Patel: Quick question — do we have automated tests for regressions integrated in Redwood?
[10:56] Jordan Lee: We have quality monitoring and regression alerts tied to prompt sets and evals; you can push your test suite and we'll run it pre- and post-deploy.
[11:07] [00:12:00] Ethan Park: About the GPU memory layouts, you mentioned some quant formats change KV packing — does that affect multi-GPU sharding?
[11:14] Jordan Lee: It can. Row-wise formats like GPTQ may require different partitioning strategies. Our serving runtime handles model sharding but for custom on-prem infra we might need to adjust chunk sizes. We'll share best-practice configs.
[11:28] Maya Patel: Any recommended tooling for running GPTQ locally?
[11:31] Priya Kapoor: We maintain scripts that wrap community GPTQ tools with our recommended hyperparams. We'll hand those off and help run the first pass.
[11:40] [00:13:00] Liam Chen: For monitoring, can we get per-variant A/B metrics in real time?
[11:45] Sofia Martinez: Yes — per-route dashboards, canary metrics and automated alerts on quality/regression.
[11:51] Maya Patel: How do we handle tokenization differences when comparing variants?
[11:55] Jordan Lee: Normalize on the same tokenizer and detokenize carefully; compare downstream labels rather than raw token sequences where possible. Also run multiple seed runs for stochasticity.
[12:08] [00:14:00] Maya Patel: Are there recommended fallback latencies? i.e., if quantized p99 crosses 350ms we failover?
[12:13] Jordan Lee: Yes — you can set policy thresholds and Redwood will route to fallback model variant. We'll help set those thresholds during pilot.
[12:23] Sofia Martinez: I'll note that as an action: set fallback rules for pilot.
[12:27] [00:15:00] Maya Patel: Anything surprising about AWQ that we should watch for?
[12:31] Jordan Lee: A few things — AWQ sometimes needs per-layer tuning, and in some workloads it slightly shifts token probabilities leading to downstream extraction glitches. But it often offers a good balance of speed and accuracy when tuned.
[12:46] Liam Chen: If we prefer to not move model artifacts off-prem, can Redwood operate on images we run?
[12:51] Sofia Martinez: Yes — for Private deployments we can operate with your artifacts and we don't need to take custody of weights. We'll provide runbooks and assist remotely.
[13:03] [00:16:00] Ethan Park: For the pilot, what logs or traces should we collect to aid debugging?
[13:08] Jordan Lee: Collect per-request latency, token-level timing, KV cache hit rate, batch sizes, GPU utilization, and raw model outputs for a sample subset. Also collect system-level metrics (memory, PCI-e bandwidth) for correlation.
[13:26] Priya Kapoor: Another note — for NER we should monitor entity boundary shifts, not just token F1.
[13:32] Maya Patel: Agreed. We'll provide evaluation scripts.
[13:36] [00:17:00] Sofia Martinez: Ok wrapping toward next steps — we'll share: benchmark template, pilot contract, security docs, compatibility matrix, and kernel build notes. Jordan will run initial quant runs.
[13:52] Liam Chen: Sounds good. Any blockers from Redwood side?
[13:55] Jordan Lee: None. We just need the representative prompt set and traces plus a contact for VPC access.
[14:04] Maya Patel: I'll email those today.
[14:07] Ethan Park: I'll set up infra contact and send test creds to the Redwood team.
[14:12] [00:18:00] Sofia Martinez: Great. Let's recap action items and owners.
[14:18] Jordan Lee: I'll run int8/gptq/awq and upload results by next week.
[14:22] Maya Patel: We'll get you the trace and metric definitions by April 1.
[14:26] Sofia Martinez: I'll send the pricing and SOC2 by Monday.
[14:30] Liam Chen: Thanks everyone.
[14:33] [00:19:00] End of call.
